title: Vinita Gupta, First Indian-Origin Woman to IPO a US Company, on the Courage to Start and Start Again
excerpt: The IIT Roorkee and UCLA alumna built Digital Link Corporation in 1985 and took it public in 1994. Three decades later, her memoir and campus talks are inspiring a new generation.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Vinita Gupta became the first Indian-origin woman to IPO a US company in 1994.
  • She founded Digital Link Corporation in 1985 and led it for over two decades.
  • Her memoir, 'The Woman In Deed,' chronicles her journey and was celebrated at the Computer History Museum.
  • Gupta emphasizes resilience and problem-solving in her talks to students.
  • She holds two US patents and serves on multiple boards in the tech and health sectors.

Article on Vinita Gupta's achievements
  • Vinita Gupta became the first woman of Indian origin to take a US company public when Digital Link Corporation completed its IPO in 1994
  • An IIT Roorkee and UCLA alumna, she founded the telecommunications company in 1985 and led it as chair, president and CEO for over two decades
  • Her memoir, "The Woman In Deed: Road to IPO, Bridge Tables, and Beyond," was published last fall and celebrated at the Computer History Museum
  • She recently returned to UCLA for a fireside chat, telling students: "You put one foot in front of the other, knock down each problem as it pops up"

Before Indra Nooyi ran PepsiCo, before Jayshree Ullal built Arista Networks into a $100 billion company, Vinita Gupta was quietly making history in Silicon Valley. In 1994, the Delhi-born engineer became the first woman of Indian origin to take a company public in the United States — a milestone that still defines the outer edge of what was possible for Indian women in American tech.

From IIT Roorkee to IPO

Gupta earned her bachelor's degree in electronics and communications engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee in 1973 — one of very few women in her class. She arrived in the United States the following year and became the only woman in her cohort to graduate from UCLA with a master's in electrical engineering.

After stints at GTE Lenkurt and Bell Northern Research, she founded Digital Link Corporation in May 1985, a company that designed, manufactured and marketed digital wide-area network access products for global networks. The company went public in 1994, and Gupta served as its only chairman, president and CEO through its later incarnation as Quick Eagle Networks until her retirement around 2016.

She holds two US patents — a solid-state relay (1984) and a square root circuit (1986) — and sits on the boards of the Palo Alto Medical Foundation, the Indian School of Business in Hyderabad, and the Cancer Prevention Institute of California.

'One Foot in Front of the Other'

Gupta returned to UCLA in May at the invitation of Women Advancing Technology Through Teamwork (WATT), a student group, for a fireside chat with faculty and students.

"You put one foot in front of the other, knock down each problem as it pops up, and one day you may emerge a winner."

— Vinita Gupta, at UCLA Samueli School of Engineering

Her memoir, The Woman In Deed: Road to IPO, Bridge Tables, and Beyond, published last fall, chronicles her journey from India to Silicon Valley. It was celebrated at a launch event at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, with Rubrik co-founder Bipul Sinha as chief guest and a fireside chat with pioneering investor Kanwal Rekhi.

The book includes episodes that capture the particular texture of her experience — Forbes once documented the time she went into labor during a board meeting — alongside reflections on raising her daughters and navigating family health crises while running a public company.

The Path She Opened

Gupta's career predates the wave of Indian-origin executives who now run some of America's largest companies. Her story is a reminder that the diaspora's presence in US tech leadership did not begin with the current generation of CEOs — it was built by founders who arrived with engineering degrees and the conviction that they could compete on equal terms.

The UK House of Commons recognized Gupta for her contributions to the tech industry last November. In retirement, she has shifted her focus to competitive bridge and writing, but continues to mentor young entrepreneurs through speaking engagements.

"This book is not just about my professional milestones," she said at the Computer History Museum. "It is about vulnerability, resilience, and the courage to start anew."
